q: The domain controller that holds the PDC Emulator role for contoso.local was destroyed in a fire and cannot be recovered. A healthy writable domain controller, DC2, remains in the same domain. You need the role available on DC2 now. What should you do?
opts: Transfer the role to DC2 with the same cmdlet but without -Force, so it moves gracefully
Raise the domain functional level so AD DS reassigns the role to the newest DC
Seize the role onto DC2 by running Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole with -Force
Re-promote a replacement server that uses the failed DC's name so it reclaims the role
why: FSMO roles never fail over on their own. When the holder is permanently gone you seize the role onto a surviving DC, which Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole does when you add -Force (ntdsutil can do the same). Running the cmdlet without -Force attempts a graceful transfer, which cannot complete because the current holder is unreachable. A rebuilt server with the same name has no claim on a role that was never cleanly moved. Functional levels gate features and never reassign operations master roles. After seizing, the failed DC must never be brought back online with its old identity.

q: Two AD DS sites are connected by a WAN site link. Inter-site replication must run only between 22:00 and 06:00, and once every 60 minutes inside that window, to protect daytime bandwidth. Which two site link settings should you configure? (Choose two.)
opts: The cost of the site link
A site link bridge between the two sites
The preferred bridgehead server in each site
The replication interval of the site link
The replication schedule of the site link
why: The schedule defines the hours during which the link may replicate, and the interval defines how often replication occurs inside those hours (180 minutes by default). Cost only ranks links when several paths exist, so it doesn't change timing. A preferred bridgehead picks which DC does the replicating, not when. A site link bridge makes links transitive, which is irrelevant with just two sites. Intra-site replication, by contrast, uses change notification and ignores these settings.

q: Contoso and Fabrikam each run an AD forest with several domains and are merging. Users in every Fabrikam domain need access to resources in every Contoso domain. Contoso users must not gain access to Fabrikam resources. Which trust should you create?
opts: A two-way forest trust between the two forest root domains
A one-way forest trust in which Fabrikam is the trusting forest and Contoso is the trusted forest
A one-way forest trust in which Contoso is the trusting forest and Fabrikam is the trusted forest
A one-way external trust between the two forest root domains
why: Resources live in the trusting side and users live in the trusted side, so Contoso (resources) must trust Fabrikam (users), and a forest trust is transitive across every domain in both forests. The reverse one-way forest trust would give Contoso users access to Fabrikam instead. A two-way forest trust gives both directions, which violates the restriction. An external trust is non-transitive and would reach only the two root domains, leaving the other domains out.

q: A domain-linked GPO sets the screen lock timeout to 15 minutes. Two GPOs are linked to the Finance OU, and none is Enforced: GPO-Lockdown (link order 2) sets 5 minutes, and GPO-Standard (link order 1) sets 10 minutes. What timeout applies to computers in the Finance OU?
opts: 10 minutes, because link order 1 has the highest precedence among the GPOs linked to the OU
5 minutes, because the most restrictive value wins a conflict between GPOs
15 minutes, because the domain-linked GPO covers the broadest scope
5 minutes, because the highest link order number is processed last and wins
why: Policy applies in Local, Site, Domain, OU order, so the OU-linked GPOs override the domain GPO. Inside one container, the GPO with the lowest link order number has the highest precedence (it is applied last), so GPO-Standard at link order 1 wins with 10 minutes. The higher link order number is applied earlier and is overwritten. Broader scope does not win; the closest container does. Group Policy has no most-restrictive-wins rule; precedence alone decides.

q: A branch office has an unsecured server closet and an unreliable WAN link. Users there must still sign in when the link is down, and the security team requires that a stolen server expose only the credentials of branch users and computers. What should you deploy?
opts: A writable domain controller protected with BitLocker and a TPM
A writable domain controller with Credential Guard enabled
Universal group membership caching for the branch site, without a local domain controller
An RODC with a Password Replication Policy limited to the local office's accounts
why: An RODC authenticates locally and caches only the credentials its Password Replication Policy permits, so theft exposes just those accounts. A writable DC holds every account's secrets in the AD database; BitLocker protects the disk only while the machine is off or the volume is locked, and doesn't reduce what the DC stores. Credential Guard protects LSASS secrets in memory, not the contents of the AD database. Universal group membership caching only caches group membership, and with no local DC the users could not sign in at all while the WAN is down.

q: Four load-balanced IIS servers must run an application pool under one service identity whose password AD rotates automatically. You plan to create a group managed service account in a newly built forest that has never hosted one. What must you do in the forest before New-ADServiceAccount will succeed?
opts: Raise the forest functional level to Windows Server 2025
Run Install-ADServiceAccount on each of the four IIS servers
Create a KDS root key by running Add-KdsRootKey
Create a Password Settings Object that rotates the service account password
why: A gMSA's password is derived from the Key Distribution Service root key, so the forest needs a KDS root key (Add-KdsRootKey) before the account can be created; production forests normally wait for the key to replicate, while a lab can use -EffectiveImmediately. Install-ADServiceAccount is a later step, run on each host after the account exists and the hosts are authorized to retrieve its password. A Password Settings Object governs user password policy, whereas AD manages a gMSA password on its own. The forest functional level is not the gate for gMSAs.

q: A domain administrator's password can be cached on a branch RODC simply by adding that administrator's account to the Allowed RODC Password Replication Group.
opts: True
False
why: Privileged groups such as Domain Admins are members of the Denied RODC Password Replication Group, and an explicit deny always overrides an allow in the Password Replication Policy. The administrator's credentials are therefore never cached on the RODC no matter what allow entry is added, which is deliberate so a stolen branch server cannot expose high-privilege credentials.

q: Two GPOs are linked to the domain: Security-Baseline (Enforced) and Desktop-Theme (not Enforced). The Marketing OU has Block Inheritance enabled and has its own linked GPO, Marketing-Apps. Which GPOs apply to computers in the Marketing OU?
opts: Security-Baseline, Desktop-Theme, and Marketing-Apps
Desktop-Theme and Marketing-Apps
Security-Baseline and Marketing-Apps
Marketing-Apps, with both domain GPOs blocked
why: Block Inheritance stops non-enforced GPOs linked above the OU from applying, but an Enforced GPO still flows through, and the OU's own linked GPO always applies. So Security-Baseline and Marketing-Apps apply. Marketing-Apps alone would be the result only if Security-Baseline were not Enforced. Applying all three ignores Block Inheritance entirely, and Desktop-Theme with Marketing-Apps reverses the effect of Enforced.

q: The domain controller that holds both the Schema Master and Domain Naming Master roles is offline, and no other FSMO roles are affected. Which two tasks will fail until those roles are restored or seized? (Choose two.)
opts: Adding a new child domain to the forest
Creating new user accounts in an existing domain
Extending the AD schema for a new application
Resetting a user's password in an existing domain
why: The Schema Master is the only DC that accepts schema changes, and the Domain Naming Master is the only DC that can add or remove domains in the forest. Creating users depends on the RID Master only when a DC's RID pool runs out, and password resets depend on the PDC Emulator for urgent replication; neither relies on the two forest-wide roles that are offline.

q: An OU named Sales and all its user accounts were deleted three days ago. The AD Recycle Bin has been enabled for a year. You must return the users to their original OU with their group memberships intact. What should you restore first?
opts: The user accounts' tombstones, reanimated with ldp.exe
The Sales OU object, followed by its deleted child objects
The user accounts first, with Restore-ADObject recreating the Sales OU on demand
The domain controller's system state, in Directory Services Restore Mode
why: Restore-ADObject needs the object's parent container to exist, so the deleted OU must come back before its children can return to it; the Recycle Bin then restores each user with its link-valued attributes, including group memberships. Restoring users first fails because the original parent is still deleted and Restore-ADObject does not recreate it. A system state restore in DSRM is heavier than needed and can roll back unrelated changes. Tombstone reanimation recovers bare objects that have lost group memberships.

q: A branch site has one domain controller that is not a global catalog. In your multi-domain forest, branch users who belong to universal groups sometimes cannot sign in while the WAN link is down. You want to avoid making that DC a global catalog because of the replication traffic. What should you enable?
opts: Universal group membership caching for the branch site
A longer replication interval on the site link to the branch
The Infrastructure Master role on the branch domain controller
A shortcut trust between the branch domain and the forest root domain
why: Universal group membership can only be resolved by a global catalog. Universal group membership caching lets the branch DC cache a user's universal group memberships after the first sign-in, so later sign-ins succeed even when no GC is reachable, without the cost of a full GC replica. The Infrastructure Master fixes cross-domain references and plays no part in sign-in. A shortcut trust shortens referral paths, and a longer replication interval changes timing, not GC availability.

q: You are about to enable the AD Recycle Bin in a forest. Which two statements about the feature are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It is enabled automatically when the forest functional level is raised to Windows Server 2016
Once enabled, the feature cannot be disabled again for the forest
Objects deleted before the feature was enabled can be restored with their group memberships intact
The forest functional level must be Windows Server 2008 R2 or higher before it can be enabled
why: The Recycle Bin is turned on deliberately with Enable-ADOptionalFeature, requires a forest functional level of at least Windows Server 2008 R2, and is irreversible. It only protects objects deleted after it is enabled; anything deleted earlier is an ordinary tombstone that has lost most link-valued attributes such as group memberships. Raising the functional level makes the feature available but never enables it automatically.

q: One AD forest contains two trees: contoso.com with the child domain sales.contoso.com, and fabrikam.com with the child domain eu.fabrikam.com. Users in eu.fabrikam.com often access resources in sales.contoso.com, and sign-ins are slow because requests walk up and down both domain trees. What should you add to shorten the authentication path?
opts: A realm trust between eu.fabrikam.com and sales.contoso.com
A forest trust between fabrikam.com and contoso.com
A site link between the sites hosting the two domains' domain controllers
A shortcut trust between eu.fabrikam.com and sales.contoso.com
why: Trusts within a forest are transitive through the tree hierarchy, so cross-tree requests are referred up to the roots and back down. A shortcut trust gives the two domains a direct path and removes those referral hops. A forest trust connects two separate forests, and these domains are already in one forest. A realm trust links a domain to a non-Windows Kerberos realm. A site link controls replication topology and does nothing for authentication referrals.

q: An administrator deleted an OU containing 200 users, and the deletion has replicated to every domain controller. The AD Recycle Bin was never enabled. Last night's system state backup of a DC still contains the OU. Which procedure brings the OU back without replication deleting it again?
opts: Restore the backup in DSRM, then mark the OU subtree as authoritative with ntdsutil
Restore the backup in DSRM and allow normal replication to finish, without marking anything authoritative
Reanimate the OU and each user tombstone with ldp.exe
Enable the AD Recycle Bin and then run Restore-ADObject against the deleted OU
why: An authoritative restore, done in Directory Services Restore Mode with ntdsutil, raises the version of the restored OU subtree so it replicates out and overwrites the deletion on every other DC. A non-authoritative restore lets partners replicate the deletion straight back. Enabling the Recycle Bin now does not help because it only protects objects deleted after it is enabled. Tombstone reanimation recovers bare objects without group memberships and without the OU hierarchy intact.

q: Microsoft Entra Domain Services synchronizes in both directions with on-premises AD DS, so a change made to an object in the managed domain is written back to the on-premises domain.
opts: True
False
why: Synchronization into the managed domain is one-way, from Microsoft Entra ID (which itself receives on-premises identities through Microsoft Entra Connect or Cloud Sync) to the Entra Domain Services domain. Changes made inside the managed domain are not written back to on-premises AD DS. The managed domain is a separate, Microsoft-operated AD DS environment for legacy apps that need domain join, Kerberos, NTLM, or Group Policy.

q: You plan to move the Sales-Laptops OU under a different parent OU. Before moving it, you must predict which GPOs would apply to one laptop account in that OU after the move. The laptop is currently offline. Which tool should you use?
opts: Group Policy Modeling in GPMC
gpupdate /force run on the laptop
Group Policy Results in GPMC
gpresult /h run on the laptop
why: Group Policy Modeling simulates the GPOs that would apply to a user or computer in a chosen OU, site, and security-group scenario without needing the target online, which suits a what-if before a move. Group Policy Results and gpresult report what actually applied on a real target, so they cannot predict a change that has not happened and need access to the machine. gpupdate /force only refreshes policy and reports nothing.

q: A team deploys a new domain controller as an Azure VM. The AD database, logs, and SYSVOL are on the OS disk, the VM has a dynamic private IP and a public IP for convenience, and it is the only DC in the region. Which change set matches Microsoft's guidance?
opts: Convert the VM to a scale set so the DC is recreated automatically if it fails, and keep the public IP for administration
Keep the AD files on the OS disk with ReadWrite caching, reserve the public IP, and rely on Azure Backup instead of a second DC
Move NTDS.dit, logs, and SYSVOL to a separate data disk with host caching None, use a static private IP, remove the public IP, and deploy a second DC in another zone
Place the AD files on the temporary disk so they are fast, keep the dynamic address, and add a second DC in the same availability zone
why: The AD database engine manages its own write ordering, so its files belong on a separate persistent data disk with host caching set to None. DCs get static private IPs, never public IPs, and at least two DCs should sit in different zones or an availability set. The temporary disk is not persistent, ReadWrite caching can interfere with database consistency, and a scale set is not a way to run a domain controller.

q: Two domain controllers in an Azure virtual network also act as DNS servers. After a reboot, one DC is slow to start its services, and its adapter lists only 127.0.0.1 as the DNS server. What is the recommended configuration?
opts: Set the virtual network's custom DNS servers to the DCs and keep the loopback address only as a secondary or tertiary DNS entry on each DC
Add a public DNS server as the first entry on each DC so it can always resolve names
Remove DNS from the DCs and point the VMs at the Azure-provided resolver for AD names
List the loopback address first on every DC so it always resolves itself quickly
why: A DC that points only to itself, or to itself first, can delay startup because the services it needs may not be ready; the loopback address should be secondary or tertiary, with a partner DC first, and the VNet-level custom DNS setting lets other VMs find the DCs. The Azure-provided resolver cannot answer AD SRV records, and a public resolver cannot resolve internal AD zones.

q: In a Windows Server 2025 domain, a legacy line-of-business service runs on one server under a service account with a static password that has been shared widely. The team wants to replace that account with a machine-bound identity that has managed, randomized keys and make the old password stop working. What should they use?
opts: A fine-grained password policy with a longer minimum length on the existing account
A group managed service account shared by several servers
A delegated managed service account created to replace the existing service account
A new standard user account with the password rotated every quarter
why: A dMSA can replace an existing service account: authentication with the old password is blocked and redirected through the LSA to the dMSA, whose keys are randomized and tied to the machine. A gMSA gives one identity across multiple servers and is not the device-bound replacement the scenario describes. A stricter password policy or quarterly rotation still leaves a human-known password in play.

q: After a failed restore, several domain controllers have an empty SYSVOL. One DC holds a known good SYSVOL copy replicated by DFSR. How is the good copy made authoritative for the others?
opts: Delete the DFS Replication database on every DC so that each rebuilds from scratch
Copy the SYSVOL folder to each DC with robocopy and restart the Netlogon service
Raise the domain functional level so SYSVOL replication is re-initialized
Set msDFSR-Options to 1 on that DC's SYSVOL Subscription object, restart the DFSR service, and verify event ID 4602
why: Marking one DC's SYSVOL subscription authoritative by setting msDFSR-Options to 1 and restarting DFSR makes the others re-sync from it, and event 4602 confirms it. Copying files by hand bypasses replication metadata, deleting databases everywhere discards the good copy's authority and is discouraged, and a functional level change does not re-initialize SYSVOL.

q: A domain-joined member server restored from an old snapshot rejects domain logons with 'the trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed', but a local administrator can sign in. Which action fixes it without removing the server from the domain?
opts: Run Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair with domain credentials, or Reset-ComputerMachinePassword
Run repadmin /syncall against the server so it pulls the current account data
Run gpupdate /force so the server refreshes its computer policy
Run w32tm /resync so the server's clock matches the domain again
why: The snapshot carries an older computer account password than the domain now holds, so the secure channel breaks; repairing it resets the computer account password without rejoining. repadmin acts on domain controller replication, gpupdate refreshes policy over a channel that is already broken, and a time resync helps Kerberos clock skew, not a mismatched machine password.

q: Intermittent Kerberos failures began after a virtual machine was restored and its clock is 12 minutes behind the domain controllers. Which explanation and fix is correct?
opts: The VM must be rejoined to the domain, because a clock difference always breaks the computer account
Kerberos does not depend on time, so the cause is a missing SPN and the fix is setspn -S
Kerberos tolerates up to 15 minutes by default, so the cause must be DNS and the fix is ipconfig /flushdns
The clock exceeds the default 5-minute Kerberos tolerance, so resynchronize time from the domain hierarchy with w32tm /resync
why: Kerberos tickets carry timestamps, and a skew above the default 5 minutes causes failures, so correct the time source and resync. The 15-minute figure is wrong, SPNs matter for service authentication but do not explain a clock-driven failure, and time skew does not damage the computer account, so rejoining is unnecessary.

q: An administrator wants a quick forest-wide view of which domain controllers are failing inbound replication and what the largest replication delta is. Which command provides it?
opts: repadmin /replsummary
dcdiag /test:dns on a single member server
gpresult /r
nltest /sc_query:contoso.com
why: repadmin /replsummary summarizes replication results across DCs, listing failures and the largest delta. gpresult reports Group Policy results, nltest /sc_query checks one machine's secure channel, and a DNS test on a member server does not report DC replication status.

q: Time in an Active Directory forest must come from one authoritative internal source that is configured to synchronize with an external NTP server. Which domain controller should that be?
opts: The infrastructure master of any child domain
Any global catalog server
The RID master of the forest root domain
The PDC emulator of the forest root domain
why: Domain members sync through the domain hierarchy up to the PDC emulator of the forest root, which is therefore the place to configure an external time source. The RID master, infrastructure master, and global catalog roles have nothing to do with time.

q: Data residency rules require 40 Windows Servers to stay in your datacenter. You must evaluate them with Azure Policy and Microsoft Defender for Cloud, with the least effort and without moving any workload. What should you do?
opts: Install Azure Monitor Agent on each server without enabling Azure Arc
Onboard the servers to Azure Arc by installing the Connected Machine agent
Replicate the servers to Azure VMs with Azure Migrate and then cut them over
Provision ExpressRoute so Azure management services can reach the servers
why: Azure Arc projects each server into Azure Resource Manager as a resource, which is what Azure Policy and Defender for Cloud target, and the workload never moves. Azure Migrate relocates the workload into Azure, which the residency rule forbids. For non-Azure servers Azure Monitor Agent is itself delivered as an Arc extension, so installing it alone creates no resource that policy can evaluate. ExpressRoute only supplies network connectivity; it does not make a server an Azure resource.

q: You manage 25 servers, several running Server Core. Administrators use locked-down laptops where no software can be installed, and they want a graphical management tool that runs in a browser without opening RDP sessions to each server. What should you deploy?
opts: PowerShell remoting with Enter-PSSession from each laptop
Server Manager on a jump server that administrators reach over RDP
Remote Server Administration Tools on each administrator's laptop
Windows Admin Center in gateway mode on a management server
why: Windows Admin Center installed as a gateway serves a browser-based GUI that manages Server Core and Desktop Experience servers alike, so nothing has to be installed on the laptops. RSAT is a client-side install and uses MMC consoles rather than a browser. Server Manager on a jump server still depends on RDP, which the requirement excludes. Enter-PSSession is a command-line experience, not a graphical one.

q: A six-node Hyper-V failover cluster must install monthly updates automatically on a schedule, one node at a time, draining each node first. No separate computer should be needed to orchestrate the runs. What should you configure?
opts: Cluster-Aware Updating in remote-updating mode, run from a dedicated update coordinator server
Cluster-Aware Updating in self-updating mode, with the CAU clustered role added to the cluster
WSUS auto-approval with a deadline so each node installs and restarts on its own
A Group Policy that sets an automatic installation time for the cluster nodes
why: In self-updating mode the CAU clustered role lives on the cluster and runs the update runs on a schedule, draining and patching one node at a time with no outside coordinator. Remote-updating mode relies on a separate update coordinator computer, which the requirement rules out. Group Policy or WSUS deadlines make each node install and restart independently, with no coordination and no drain, so several nodes can go down at once.

q: Two standalone Hyper-V hosts in different cities have no cluster and no shared storage. One VM must have a copy at the second site that is never more than five minutes behind. Other VMs on the same volumes must not be replicated. What should you configure?
opts: The Hyper-V Replica Broker role on each host, then replication for that VM
Hyper-V Replica for that VM, using the 30-second or 5-minute replication frequency
Storage Replica between the volumes that hold the VM on both hosts
Shared-nothing Live Migration of that VM to the second host on a five-minute schedule
why: Hyper-V Replica works between standalone hosts, replicates a chosen VM asynchronously, and offers 30-second, 5-minute, and 15-minute frequencies. Storage Replica replicates whole volumes, so every VM on them would be copied, and its destination volume is not usable until failover. The Replica Broker role is only for clustered hosts and is not needed here. Live Migration moves a VM rather than keeping a copy of it, so repeating it is not a replication strategy.

q: On Windows Server 2022, you can convert a Server Core installation to Desktop Experience in place by adding the Server-Gui-Shell feature.
opts: True
False
why: Starting with Windows Server 2016 the installation option cannot be switched in place; changing between Server Core and Desktop Experience means a new installation or a migration. Server-Gui-Shell worked on Windows Server 2012 R2, which is why the myth persists. Server Core is meant to be managed remotely with Windows Admin Center, PowerShell, or RSAT.

q: You plan to move 200 on-premises Hyper-V VMs to Azure over the next year. Before migrating, you need to discover the VMs, review their readiness, and get right-sized Azure VM recommendations with cost estimates. Which service should you start with?
opts: Azure Update Manager with maintenance schedules
Azure Migrate discovery and assessment
Azure Arc-enabled servers with the Connected Machine agent
Azure Site Recovery with Hyper-V replication to Azure
why: Azure Migrate's discovery and assessment tooling inventories on-premises VMs and produces readiness, sizing, and cost recommendations before a move. Azure Arc manages servers where they are and does not plan or perform a migration. Azure Site Recovery replicates VMs for disaster recovery or migration but does not produce sizing and readiness assessments. Azure Update Manager handles patching only.

q: Which three statements about Azure Arc-enabled servers are true? (Choose three.)
opts: The server needs a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute connection before it can be onboarded
An Arc-enabled server receives an Azure resource ID, so Azure RBAC and tags can apply to it
Azure Policy and Defender for Cloud can evaluate it the same way as a native Azure VM
The Connected Machine agent connects outbound to Azure, and can use a proxy or Private Link
After onboarding, the server's workload runs on Azure compute and is billed as an Azure VM
why: The Connected Machine agent initiates outbound connections to Azure endpoints, optionally through a proxy or Private Link, and each Arc-enabled server becomes a resource with an ID, resource group, RBAC, and tags, which is what lets Azure Policy and Defender for Cloud evaluate it like an Azure VM. No VPN or ExpressRoute is required for onboarding. Arc projects the server into Azure Resource Manager for management only; the workload stays on its own hardware and is not billed as an Azure VM.

q: Which two statements correctly compare an in-place upgrade with a migration to a new server? (Choose two.)
opts: A migration requires the source and destination servers to run the same Windows Server version
An in-place upgrade can switch the installation from Server Core to Desktop Experience
A migration lets you move from Desktop Experience to Server Core on the destination server
An in-place upgrade keeps the server's name, IP address, roles, and data on the same hardware or VM
why: An in-place upgrade updates the OS on the existing machine and so preserves its identity, roles, and data, but it cannot change the installation option. A migration moves roles and data to a separately built destination, which is why you can choose a different installation option, a newer version, or new hardware there. Migrations are not limited to matching versions, and an in-place upgrade cannot convert Server Core into Desktop Experience.

q: A two-node failover cluster spans two small branch offices, and no third site is available for a witness. The cluster must stay online if either office loses power. Which quorum witness fits?
opts: A disk witness on shared storage located in one of the two offices
Node Majority alone, because two nodes together already form a majority
A file share witness hosted on a file server in one of the two offices
Cloud Witness, using a small Azure Storage account instead of a third physical site
why: With two nodes, losing one leaves a single vote out of two, which is not a majority, so a witness vote is required. Cloud Witness supplies it from Azure Blob Storage, outside both offices, so losing either office still leaves two of three votes. A disk or file share witness hosted in one office fails together with that office, taking a node and the witness out at once and dropping the cluster to one of three votes. Having no witness leaves the cluster down after a single node failure.

q: A production Hyper-V failover cluster passed validation when it was built. Which two changes should prompt you to run cluster validation again to stay in a supported configuration? (Choose two.)
opts: Adding a new node to the cluster
Installing the monthly cumulative update through Cluster-Aware Updating
Updating the multipath driver and firmware on the shared storage array
Renaming a clustered virtual machine role
why: Cluster validation tests the hardware, storage, and network configuration, so it should be repeated whenever those change, such as adding a node or changing the storage driver and firmware stack. A routine cumulative update applied by Cluster-Aware Updating, or renaming a clustered role, does not alter the hardware, storage, or network configuration that validation checks. A cluster that skips or fails validation can still run but is treated as unsupported if a validation-related problem later causes an outage.

q: A Hyper-V Replica primary host needs scheduled maintenance. You must move the VM to the replica host at the secondary site with no data loss, and replication must reverse so the original host becomes the new replica afterward. What should you do?
opts: Break the replication relationship and start the replica VM manually
Shut down the primary VM and run a planned failover, selecting the option to reverse replication
Run a test failover and then promote the resulting test VM to production
Run an unplanned failover on the replica while the primary VM keeps running
why: A planned failover shuts down the primary VM, sends the last pending changes so nothing is lost, starts the replica, and can reverse replication so the original host becomes the replica. An unplanned failover is the emergency path for an unreachable primary and can lose changes made since the last replication cycle, while a still-running primary would create two active copies. A test failover builds a separate temporary VM that cannot be promoted. Breaking replication loses the final changes and any reverse relationship.

q: You Arc-enable 30 on-premises Windows Servers. All show as Connected in the Azure portal, but Azure Update Manager lists no update compliance data for them. What should you do?
opts: Migrate the servers to Azure VMs, because Update Manager reports only on native Azure VMs
Associate a data collection rule that collects update events with the servers
Turn on periodic assessment for the servers so Update Manager checks for missing updates automatically
Remove the WSUS configuration so Update Manager can reach the Microsoft update service
why: Arc-enabling a server makes it an Azure resource, but Update Manager still needs an assessment to run before compliance data appears; periodic assessment makes that happen automatically on a schedule. Update Manager supports Arc-enabled servers directly, so no migration to Azure VMs is needed. Update compliance does not come from a data collection rule, and an existing WSUS configuration does not stop Update Manager from assessing a server.

q: A hosting provider has outgrown the node limit of a single failover cluster. It needs one larger compute and storage pool, and VMs must live-migrate between its clusters. Which feature should it deploy?
opts: Hyper-V Replica between the clusters
A cluster set that groups the member clusters into one fabric
A single Storage Spaces Direct cluster scaled to its maximum of 16 nodes
A stretched cluster with Storage Replica between two sites
why: A cluster set groups several independent failover clusters into one fabric, so capacity scales beyond a single cluster and VMs can live-migrate across member clusters. A Storage Spaces Direct cluster is still one cluster bounded by its 16-node ceiling. A stretched cluster spreads one cluster over two sites for resilience and does not raise the node limit. Hyper-V Replica provides asynchronous disaster recovery copies, not live migration or pooled capacity.

q: A VM replicates from Site A to Site B with Hyper-V Replica. Management wants a third copy of the VM at Site C. Where do you configure the additional replication?
opts: On the replica server at Site B, enabling extended replication for the replica VM
At Site C, by pulling changes from the primary VM across both WAN links
On the primary server at Site A, after removing the existing Site B relationship
On the primary server at Site A, adding Site C as a second replica of the same VM
why: Extended replication is chained: the replica VM at Site B replicates onward to Site C, layered on top of the working A-to-B pair. A primary VM supports only one replica, so Site C cannot be added as a second replica from Site A. Hyper-V Replica is push-based, so Site C cannot pull changes. Removing the Site B relationship is unnecessary and would leave no replica while Site C is being seeded.

q: A team onboards Azure Arc-enabled servers and wants one profile that applies Microsoft-recommended settings for Defender, update management, and Change Tracking, and automatically corrects any local drift. Which service should they enable?
opts: Azure Automanage, using a best-practices configuration profile
Azure Monitor, with a data collection rule for each server
Azure Update Manager, with a maintenance schedule for each server
Microsoft Defender for Cloud, with the Defender for Servers plan
why: Azure Automanage bundles several services, including Defender, update management, and Change Tracking, into one profile and re-applies it if a setting drifts, for both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. Update Manager covers only patching, Defender for Servers covers only security protection, and Azure Monitor with a data collection rule covers only data collection. Each would still leave the other services to configure by hand.

q: Which two statements about Azure Automanage are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It supports only machines running in Azure, so Arc-enabled servers need Azure Policy instead
It can apply its configuration profile to both Azure VMs and Azure Arc-enabled servers
A non-Azure server must first be converted into an Azure VM with Azure Migrate before onboarding
It corrects configuration drift from the profile on onboarded machines automatically
why: Automanage works on Azure VMs and on Arc-enabled servers, and its defining behavior is continuously re-applying the profile when a setting drifts. It does not exclude Arc-enabled machines, and a non-Azure server only needs to be Arc-enabled, not migrated into Azure, because Automanage builds on the Arc resource.

q: Admins must manage an Arc-enabled Windows Server in a branch office from the Azure portal using Windows Admin Center. The branch has no VPN, no public IP, and no inbound firewall openings. What is required?
opts: Create an ExpressRoute circuit to the branch and use Azure Bastion for the session
Install a Windows Admin Center gateway on every admin workstation
Open inbound TCP 6516 on the branch firewall and publish the server's public IP
Install the Windows Admin Center VM extension, allow outbound HTTPS to the Windows Admin Center service, and assign the Windows Admin Center Administrator Login role
why: The portal experience works through an extension on the Arc-enabled machine, which only needs outbound HTTPS, and access is controlled with the Windows Admin Center Administrator Login role (plus Reader). Opening inbound ports or building private circuits is exactly what the feature avoids, and workstation gateways are the on-premises model, not the Azure portal one.

q: An admin runs Invoke-Command against SERVER-A. Inside the script block, the code opens a share on SERVER-B and fails with access denied, though the admin has rights on SERVER-B. Security forbids CredSSP. Which approach solves the second hop?
opts: Configure resource-based Kerberos constrained delegation on SERVER-B so SERVER-A may delegate
Enable CredSSP on both servers for just this task
Add the admin account to Protected Users to harden the session
Run Enable-PSRemoting on SERVER-B
why: Resource-based constrained delegation, configured on the second server with PrincipalsAllowedToDelegateToAccount, lets SERVER-A act for the caller toward SERVER-B without exposing credentials. CredSSP is the option security has ruled out, Protected Users actively blocks delegation, and the remoting service on SERVER-B is not the problem because the first hop already works.

q: Which two statements about the PowerShell second-hop problem are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Kerberos delegation works for any account, including Protected Users members
Accounts marked 'sensitive and cannot be delegated' cannot use delegation to make the second hop
A JEA endpoint cannot run commands that access other servers
CredSSP is disabled by default on both client and server
why: CredSSP must be enabled explicitly, and accounts flagged as sensitive cannot be delegated. Members of Protected Users also cannot be delegated, and JEA can actually help because its virtual or group managed service account can authenticate to the second hop.

q: An admin wants SSH access to a freshly installed Windows Server 2025 machine. What is true about OpenSSH on this release?
opts: It runs only after WinRM is configured over HTTPS on TCP 5986
It is not installed, so it must be added with Add-WindowsCapability before sshd can be started
The server component is installed but not enabled, so start sshd, set it to automatic, and allow TCP 22
It is enabled and listening by default, so only a key pair is needed
why: Windows Server 2025 ships OpenSSH installed but not enabled. Installing it as an optional feature was required on Windows Server 2019 and 2022. It is not listening by default, and SSH has no dependency on WinRM.

q: For an account that is a member of the local Administrators group, OpenSSH on Windows reads authorized public keys from that user's own .ssh\authorized_keys file.
opts: True
False
why: For administrators, OpenSSH on Windows uses %programdata%\ssh\administrators_authorized_keys, and that file must have permission entries only for Administrators and SYSTEM. The per-user .ssh\authorized_keys file applies to non-administrators.

q: Installing an extension on an Azure Arc-enabled server fails. After confirming with azcmagent show that the agent is connected, where should the admin look for the extension manager's error details?
opts: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx
The Storage Sync Service's registered servers page
The Application log of the Azure portal's Activity blade for the subscription only
C:\ProgramData\GuestConfig\ext_mgr_logs, especially gc_ext.log
why: The Connected Machine agent's extension manager logs to GuestConfig\ext_mgr_logs, and gc_ext.log records download and verification errors, while the extension's own files live under C:\Packages\Plugins. The Security log records logons, not extension failures, and the Storage Sync Service page is for Azure File Sync.

q: A company wants Arc-enabled servers and Azure VMs checked for missing updates every day automatically, with installations restricted to a weekly window. Which configuration provides both?
opts: Azure Automation Update Management with a Log Analytics agent on each machine
Azure Policy machine configuration to audit the installed hotfix list
Azure Update Manager with periodic assessment enabled and a maintenance configuration for the install schedule
A WSUS server with automatic approval, and no Azure involvement
why: Update Manager's periodic assessment checks for updates every 24 hours, and a maintenance configuration defines when installation may happen, for both Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. Azure Automation Update Management is the older solution that Update Manager replaced, WSUS alone has no Azure scheduling, and machine configuration audits settings rather than orchestrating patches.

q: A Hyper-V host has two physical NICs. NIC1 carries host management traffic and NIC2 is dedicated to VM traffic. VMs need access to the physical LAN, and the host's management traffic must not pass through the virtual switch. What should you create?
opts: An external switch bound to NIC2, with 'Allow management operating system to share this network adapter' cleared
An external switch bound to NIC2, with 'Allow management operating system to share this network adapter' selected
An internal switch for the VMs, with Internet Connection Sharing enabled on NIC2
An external switch bound to NIC1, with 'Allow management operating system to share this network adapter' selected
why: Binding an external switch to NIC2 gives the VMs access to the physical LAN, and clearing the sharing option stops Hyper-V from creating a management virtual NIC on that switch, so host traffic stays on NIC1. Selecting the option adds a management vNIC to the switch and pushes host traffic through it. Binding to NIC1 would run management traffic through the virtual switch. An internal switch with Internet Connection Sharing is a NAT workaround, not direct LAN access.

q: A Generation 2 Hyper-V VM running Ubuntu Server must meet a policy that requires Secure Boot. With Secure Boot enabled, the VM fails to start and reports that the boot image failed verification. What should you change?
opts: Disable Secure Boot, because the guest operating system is Linux
Set the Secure Boot template to Microsoft UEFI Certificate Authority
Add a virtual TPM to the VM
Recreate the VM as Generation 1 and enable Secure Boot in its BIOS
why: Generation 2 VMs use the Microsoft Windows Secure Boot template by default, which does not trust the signing certificate of common Linux boot loaders. Switching the template (Set-VMFirmware with -SecureBootTemplate MicrosoftUEFICertificateAuthority) lets the Linux image verify while keeping Secure Boot enforced. A virtual TPM does not affect signature verification. Disabling Secure Boot breaks the policy, and Generation 1 VMs use legacy BIOS and have no Secure Boot at all.

q: A business-critical VM must move from one Hyper-V host to another ahead of planned host maintenance, with no perceptible downtime for connected users. The hosts' processors differ slightly in generation. Which feature should you use?
opts: Live Migration, with Processor Compatibility Mode enabled on the VM
A production checkpoint applied to a new VM created on the new host
A Hyper-V Replica planned failover to a replica copy of the VM
Exporting the VM and importing it on the new host, then starting it
why: Live Migration moves a running VM between hosts with no perceptible downtime, and Processor Compatibility Mode masks CPU feature differences between generations from the same manufacturer. A Hyper-V Replica planned failover shuts the VM down first, so users see an outage. Export and import is an offline copy followed by a restart. A checkpoint applied to a new VM is a rollback or copy technique and does not carry running state across hosts.

q: A 64-bit Windows Server 2008 R2 guest can be installed in a Generation 2 VM, because Generation 2 supports any 64-bit operating system.
opts: True
False
why: Generation 2 VMs need a UEFI-aware guest, which means 64-bit Windows Server 2012 and Windows 8 or later, plus supported Linux distributions. Windows Server 2008 R2 is 64-bit but is not UEFI-aware, so it needs a Generation 1 VM. The generation is fixed at creation, so choosing wrongly means recreating the VM.

q: Which two statements about Hyper-V Live Migration are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Both hosts must be nodes of the same failover cluster before a running VM can be moved
Processor Compatibility Mode allows moves between different CPU generations from one vendor
Processor Compatibility Mode allows moves between an Intel host and an AMD host
A VM can move between standalone hosts that share no storage, with its disks copied over the network
why: Processor Compatibility Mode masks newer CPU features so a VM can move across CPU generations from one vendor, and shared-nothing Live Migration moves a running VM and its storage between standalone hosts once authentication and migration settings are configured. The mode cannot bridge Intel and AMD, and Live Migration does not require a cluster.

q: You must take a quick rollback point of a domain controller that runs as a Hyper-V VM on Windows Server 2025, before a risky change. The rollback point must be application-consistent for AD DS and must not capture the VM's memory contents. Which should you use?
opts: A production checkpoint of the VM
Export-VM of the running VM
A standard checkpoint of the VM
A differencing disk added to the VM by hand
why: A production checkpoint asks VSS inside the guest for an application-consistent copy and does not save memory state, which is what a domain controller needs. A standard checkpoint saves memory and device state like a saved game and is not application-aware, so restoring it into a domain controller risks replication problems. Export-VM creates a separate copy rather than a rollback point on the same VM. A hand-made differencing disk is neither application-consistent nor a supported rollback mechanism.

q: A Windows Server 2022 VM is a Generation 1 VM with a full 2 TB boot VHDX. You must grow its boot volume to 4 TB. What should you do?
opts: Move the boot VHDX from the IDE controller to a SCSI controller in the same VM
Build a Generation 2 VM with a GPT boot disk and move the workload to it
Convert the boot disk to a dynamic disk and span the volume across a second VHDX
Run Resize-VHD to grow the disk to 4 TB and extend the boot volume in the guest
why: Generation 1 VMs boot through legacy BIOS from an MBR disk, which caps the boot volume at 2 TB, while Generation 2 VMs use UEFI and can boot from a GPT disk of that size. Generation cannot be changed in place, so the workload has to move. Resize-VHD enlarges the VHDX but the MBR volume still cannot exceed 2 TB. A boot or system volume cannot be spanned across disks, and a Generation 1 VM cannot boot from SCSI.

q: A hosting provider's fabric administrators have full console and hypervisor access to every Hyper-V host, but tenants require that not even those administrators be able to inspect a tenant VM's memory or disk contents. Which feature is designed specifically for this threat model?
opts: Credential Guard, isolating LSASS secrets from the fabric administrator
Shielded virtual machines, attested and key-released through the Host Guardian Service
Windows Defender Application Control, blocking unapproved code on the host
BitLocker alone, enabled on the host's own boot volume
why: Shielded VMs encrypt a tenant VM's disk and state and restrict even a fabric administrator from inspecting or console-connecting to it, with the Host Guardian Service attesting the host is trusted before releasing the needed key — exactly the hosting-provider threat model described. Credential Guard protects LSASS secrets on a single machine, not a tenant VM's contents from its own host's administrator, WDAC controls what code runs rather than who can inspect a VM, and BitLocker on the host's own boot volume doesn't protect a guest VM's contents from that host's administrators at all.

q: Which two statements about attestation for shielded VMs with the Host Guardian Service (HGS) are true? (Choose two.)
opts: HGS is normally deployed in the fabric's own domain so fabric administrators can manage it
Admin-trusted attestation requires a TPM 2.0 module in every Hyper-V host
HGS releases the key needed to start a shielded VM only after the host passes attestation
TPM-trusted attestation validates measurements that each host's TPM records at boot
why: TPM-trusted attestation depends on hardware measurements taken by each host's TPM, and HGS gates the key release on a successful attestation. Admin-trusted attestation is the weaker mode because it trusts hosts by AD group membership rather than TPM measurements, so it does not require a TPM. HGS is deliberately deployed in a separate, isolated environment so that fabric administrators cannot tamper with the service that guards their own hosts.

q: A trainer runs Hyper-V inside a VM that is connected to an external virtual switch, to simulate a host for classroom labs. Nested virtualization is enabled and the nested VMs start, but they cannot communicate with the physical LAN. What should you change on the lab VM?
opts: Move the lab VM's adapter to a private virtual switch
Enable Dynamic Memory on the lab VM so nested VMs can request memory
Enable MAC address spoofing on the lab VM's network adapter
Disable Secure Boot on the lab VM
why: Traffic from nested VMs leaves the lab VM with MAC addresses the outer virtual switch has not assigned to that adapter, and the switch drops those frames unless MAC address spoofing is allowed (alternatively, NAT can be used inside the lab VM). Dynamic Memory is not supported on a VM that has nested virtualization enabled. A private switch removes LAN access entirely, and Secure Boot has no effect on nested networking.

q: A SQL Server VM has a carefully sized buffer pool, and the database team reports unpredictable performance whenever the VM's assigned memory changes at runtime. Which Hyper-V memory configuration should you apply?
opts: Dynamic Memory, with the highest memory weight on the host
Dynamic Memory, with a higher memory buffer percentage
Dynamic Memory, with Minimum RAM equal to the startup memory
Static memory, set to the amount the buffer pool was sized for
why: Static memory fixes the allocation at one value, which suits a workload that tunes its own memory use. Every Dynamic Memory variation still lets Hyper-V raise or reclaim memory at runtime: raising the minimum, the buffer percentage, or the weight only changes how readily that happens, not whether the assigned amount can change under SQL Server.

q: You are rolling out a newer Windows Server version to a Hyper-V cluster one node at a time, and want to keep the option of reverting to the older nodes until every node is upgraded. Which two actions should you postpone until the end? (Choose two.)
opts: Running Update-VMVersion on the clustered VMs
Draining a node before it is upgraded
Live migrating VMs onto nodes that are already upgraded
Running Update-ClusterFunctionalLevel
why: Raising the cluster functional level and upgrading a VM's configuration version are both one-way steps: after them, older nodes can no longer join the cluster or host the VMs. Draining a node and live migrating VMs between old and new nodes are the normal rolling-upgrade moves and remain reversible while the VM configuration version is unchanged.

q: A Hyper-V admin must run a configuration script inside a Windows Server 2022 guest from the host. The guest has no working network adapter and WinRM is not configured. The VM runs locally on this host with a user profile. What should the admin use?
opts: Enter-PSSession -ComputerName with the guest's host name
Invoke-Command -VMName with guest credentials, using PowerShell Direct
A live migration to a host that has network access to the VM
Enhanced Session Mode to open a graphical session
why: PowerShell Direct runs commands inside the guest over the VM bus regardless of network or remote management settings, provided the guest is Windows 10 or Windows Server 2016 or later, runs locally, and the admin is a Hyper-V administrator. A computer-name session needs the network and WinRM. Enhanced Session Mode is interactive and does not run a script from the host, and live migration does not give access to the guest.

q: Edge sites running Windows Server 2025 on standalone hosts want several VDI VMs to share one physical GPU, and the VMs must be live migrated between hosts for maintenance. Hosts have IOMMU DMA bit tracking CPUs and identical supported GPUs. Which feature fits?
opts: Discrete Device Assignment of the whole GPU
Dynamic Memory on the VMs
GPU partitioning
A Generation 1 VM with a legacy network adapter
why: GPU partitioning shares one GPU across VMs through SR-IOV and, on Windows Server 2025, supports live migration when the hardware requirements are met. DDA hands the whole GPU to a single VM and blocks live migration. Dynamic Memory and legacy network adapters have nothing to do with GPU sharing.

q: A GPU is assigned to a VM with Discrete Device Assignment. Which two capabilities are unavailable for that VM while the device is attached? (Choose two.)
opts: Installing the vendor driver inside the guest
The use of Dynamic Memory
Live migration of the VM
Running as a Generation 2 VM
why: While a device is assigned, the VM cannot be live migrated, saved or restored, use Dynamic Memory, or join a high-availability cluster. DDA supports both Generation 1 and Generation 2 VMs, and installing the manufacturer's driver inside the guest is exactly how the device is used.

q: A web tier of two Azure VMs must keep running if one datacenter in the region loses power, cooling, or networking. The region supports availability zones. Which deployment achieves this?
opts: Put both VMs in one availability set with three fault domains
Use one larger VM with premium disks
Place each VM in a different availability zone behind a load balancer
Deploy both VMs in the same zone and add Azure Backup
why: Zones are physically separate datacenters, so replicas in different zones survive the loss of one. An availability set protects against rack-level and maintenance events within a datacenter location, not against losing the datacenter; backup restores data but does not keep the service running, and a single VM has no redundancy.

q: An availability set was created with five update domains and holds seven VMs. During planned maintenance, which VM restarts together with the second VM?
opts: The sixth VM, because the sixth shares an update domain with the second
The seventh VM, because it is placed in the same update domain as the second
The fifth VM, because update domains are assigned in reverse order
No other VM, because only one VM restarts at a time
why: VMs are assigned to update domains in rotation: with five update domains the sixth VM shares with the first, and the seventh shares with the second. One update domain at a time restarts, which means all its VMs restart together. The assignment is not reversed.

q: Security wants RDP and SSH ports on Azure VMs closed by default, opened only after an authorized request, only for the requester's IP address, and for a limited time. Which feature provides this?
opts: Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Servers Plan 2
A permanent NSG allow rule for the administrators' office address
Azure Backup with a restore point per request
An Azure Policy that denies public IP creation
why: JIT keeps deny rules in the NSG and Azure Firewall and, after an RBAC-checked and approved request, opens the port for the requester's address for the requested time before restoring the rules. A permanent allow rule is always open, backup is unrelated, and a policy against public IPs reduces exposure but does not provide time-boxed approved access.

q: An Azure Bastion deployment fails because the virtual network has a subnet named Bastion with a /28 prefix. What must be changed for a Standard SKU deployment?
opts: Keep the subnet name and give the VMs public IP addresses
Move Bastion into the subnet that holds the target VMs
Rename the subnet to GatewaySubnet and keep the /28 prefix
Create a subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a /26 or larger prefix in the same virtual network
why: Bastion (other than the Developer SKU) requires a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, /26 or larger, in the same virtual network. GatewaySubnet is for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, giving VMs public IPs defeats the purpose of Bastion, and it cannot share a subnet with the VMs.

q: An NSG contains an inbound rule at priority 100 that allows TCP 3389 from any source, and another at priority 200 that denies TCP 3389 from the Internet service tag. A client on the Internet connects to the VM's public IP on 3389. What happens?
opts: Both rules apply and the platform picks randomly
The connection is denied, because deny rules always win over allow rules
The connection is denied, because the higher-numbered rule is more specific
The connection is allowed, because the lower-numbered rule matches first
why: NSG rules are processed from the lowest priority number upward and processing stops at the first match, so the priority 100 allow decides. Deny rules have no special precedence, specificity does not reorder rules, and there is no random choice.

q: A forest contains corp.contoso.com and eu.corp.contoso.com, and both domains run DNS on their domain controllers. A zone for apps.contoso.com must be stored in AD, replicate to DNS servers in both domains, and accept secure dynamic updates. Which replication scope should you select?
opts: To all domain controllers in this domain, for Windows 2000 compatibility
To all DNS servers running on domain controllers in this forest
A standard primary zone with secondary zones on a DNS server in each domain
To all DNS servers running on domain controllers in this domain
why: The forest-wide scope stores the zone in the ForestDnsZones application partition, so every DNS server on a domain controller in either domain receives it, and an AD-integrated zone supports secure dynamic updates. The domain scope reaches only DNS servers in one domain. The legacy scope stores the zone in the domain partition and reaches only that domain's DCs. A standard primary zone with secondaries is not stored in AD, so it loses AD replication and secure dynamic updates.

q: A branch office needs a local DHCP server that takes over only if the WAN link fails; under normal conditions the datacenter DHCP server must answer every lease request. Which DHCP failover configuration fits?
opts: Load balance mode with a 50/50 split between the two servers
Two separate non-overlapping scopes, split 80/20 between the servers
Load balance mode with a 90/10 split favoring the datacenter server
Hot standby mode, with the datacenter server active and the branch server in standby
why: Hot standby makes one server active and keeps the other idle until the active partner becomes unavailable, which matches 'only if the WAN link fails'. Any load balance split, even 90/10, has both servers answering requests all the time, so the branch server would still serve some clients under normal conditions. Splitting the address range into two separate scopes is the old 80/20 approach; it isn't failover at all because the scopes don't share lease information.

q: Contoso needs private, predictable-latency connectivity from its datacenter to Azure virtual networks. If the dedicated circuit fails, traffic must fail over automatically to an encrypted path over the internet, at minimal added cost. What should you design?
opts: ExpressRoute as the primary path, with a site-to-site VPN gateway as the backup
A second ExpressRoute circuit from the same connectivity provider as the backup
ExpressRoute as the primary path, with point-to-site VPN connections from individual servers as backup
Two site-to-site VPN tunnels configured as active-active
why: ExpressRoute provides the private, predictable path, and a site-to-site VPN gateway can coexist with it as an encrypted internet-based failover route at modest cost. Two VPN tunnels never give a private dedicated path because both ride the public internet. Point-to-site VPN is for individual clients rather than network-to-network failover. A second circuit is private rather than internet-based and costs far more than a VPN backup.

q: DHCP failover can be configured between two Windows DHCP servers without a Windows failover cluster or any shared storage.
opts: True
False
why: A DHCP failover relationship is a partnership between two DHCP servers that replicate scope and lease information to each other, in either load balance or hot standby mode. No failover cluster or shared disk is involved, which is what distinguishes it from the older clustered DHCP approach.

q: Contoso must resolve names in partner.fabrikam.com, which is hosted on Fabrikam's DNS servers. Fabrikam occasionally changes its name servers' IP addresses. Contoso does not want to maintain a full copy of the zone or edit its own DNS configuration when those addresses change. What should Contoso configure?
opts: A conditional forwarder that lists Fabrikam's server IP addresses
A secondary zone for partner.fabrikam.com
A root hints entry for Fabrikam's name servers
A stub zone for partner.fabrikam.com
why: A stub zone holds only the NS, SOA, and glue records for the namespace and refreshes them from the zone's own name servers, so it keeps tracking address changes without storing the full record set. A conditional forwarder uses a static list of IP addresses that must be edited whenever Fabrikam changes them. A secondary zone is a full read-only copy, which Contoso does not want. Root hints describe the DNS root servers and are not used for individual zones.

q: A newly promoted domain controller cannot be located by clients. Which two record types do clients depend on to find a domain controller through DNS? (Choose two.)
opts: MX records that route mail for the domain to its mail servers
SRV records advertising the domain controller's services
A records mapping the domain controller's host name to its IP address
PTR records that map the domain controller's IP address back to its host name
why: Clients first query SRV records (such as _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs) to learn which hosts offer directory services, then resolve those host names through A records to reach them. PTR records support reverse lookups and are recommended but not required for domain controller discovery. MX records route mail and play no part in locating a DC.

q: DHCP failover runs in load balance mode with an 80/20 split favoring the datacenter server. The branch server loses its WAN link to the datacenter for several hours. What happens to DHCP service at the branch?
opts: The branch server stops answering because it depends on the datacenter server to approve each lease
Existing clients can renew leases, but new clients are not served until the partner is reachable again
The branch server converts itself to hot standby mode with the datacenter server as active
Both servers keep serving, because each partner leases from its own share of the pool while communication is interrupted
why: In load balance mode each partner owns a share of the address pool, and when the partners cannot talk, each one keeps answering from its own share and later reconciles lease information. New clients are therefore still served, not just renewals. A partner does not need approval from the other for each lease, and a failover relationship never converts itself from one mode to the other.

q: A Hyper-V host has two RDMA-capable NICs. You want to team them for converged traffic on a Hyper-V virtual switch while keeping RDMA working on the team. Which should you use?
opts: NIC teaming inside the guest operating system of each VM
An LBFO team using LACP, bound to the virtual switch
Switch Embedded Teaming (SET)
An LBFO team in switch-independent mode, bound to the virtual switch
why: Switch Embedded Teaming builds the team inside the Hyper-V virtual switch and keeps RDMA available on the teamed adapters. Classic LBFO teaming, in either switch-independent or LACP mode, is not compatible with RDMA-capable adapters. Teaming inside each guest does not combine the host's physical NICs and doesn't preserve host-side RDMA.

q: Contoso hosts app.contoso.com in two datacenters. A single AD-integrated zone on Windows Server DNS must return the nearest datacenter's IP address, based on the client's subnet. What should you configure?
opts: DNS round robin with one A record per datacenter
A DNS policy that uses client subnets and zone scopes
A conditional forwarder in each datacenter's DNS servers
A stub zone in each datacenter that points to the other
why: DNS policies choose among zone scopes, each holding its own set of records, based on criteria such as the client's subnet, so one zone can return location-specific answers. A conditional forwarder decides where to send queries for a namespace, not which stored answer to return. A stub zone only tracks the authoritative servers for a namespace. Round robin rotates addresses without any awareness of client location.

q: A company signs its internal zone with DNSSEC. Resolvers should reject forged answers, and the signed zone must not let an attacker enumerate every name by chaining 'name does not exist' answers. What combination meets this?
opts: Enable DNS policies with geo-location filters on the zone
Sign the zone with NSEC3 and distribute the trust anchor to the validating DNS servers
Encrypt the zone file with BitLocker on the DNS server
Sign the zone with NSEC and keep the trust anchor only on the authoritative server
why: NSEC3 hashes names to prevent zone walking, and validating resolvers need the zone's trust anchor to verify signatures. NSEC proves non-existence but allows enumeration, and the trust anchor must reach the validators, not stay only on the authoritative server. DNS policies and BitLocker address other problems.

q: A network printer must always receive 10.1.1.50 but should still be configured for DHCP so it is managed centrally. Which configuration is correct?
opts: An exclusion range containing 10.1.1.50, with the printer set to obtain an address automatically
A second scope that contains only 10.1.1.50
A DHCP reservation for 10.1.1.50 using the printer's MAC address
A longer lease duration on the whole scope
why: A reservation maps one address to a client's MAC address so DHCP always hands it that address. An excluded address is never leased, so a DHCP client would receive a different one. A longer lease is not a guarantee, and a one-address scope is not how a single client is pinned.

q: A new Windows Server DHCP server joined to the domain has an active scope, correct range, and a working network connection, but clients never receive leases from it. What is the most likely missing step?
opts: Raising the domain functional level
Creating a reverse lookup zone for the scope
Authorizing the DHCP server in Active Directory, for example with Add-DhcpServerInDC
Enabling SMB signing on the server
why: A DHCP server on a domain-joined computer must be authorized in AD before it will lease addresses. A reverse zone, a functional level, and SMB signing do not gate DHCP leasing.

q: Several clients on a subnet show addresses in 169.254.0.0/16. Which is the most useful first check?
opts: Whether the clients have a BitLocker recovery key
Whether DNSSEC trust anchors are present on the clients
Whether the clients' time is within Kerberos tolerance
Whether a DHCP server or relay agent can reach that subnet and the scope is active with free addresses
why: A 169.254 address means the client self-assigned an address because it received no DHCP lease, so check that DHCP is reachable and has addresses to give. Trust anchors, Kerberos time, and BitLocker are unrelated to getting a lease.

q: Users across three file servers in an AD domain must reach their folders through the single path \\contoso.com\shares. The path must stay available if any one server that hosts the namespace fails. What should you deploy?
opts: A standalone DFS namespace hosted on one of the file servers
A DFS Replication group that contains the three file servers
A domain-based DFS namespace with namespace servers on two or more file servers
Folder Redirection through Group Policy to each of the three file servers
why: A domain-based namespace is reached through the domain name and stores its configuration in AD, and adding a second namespace server keeps the path available if one fails. A standalone namespace on a single server is reached through that server's name and is a single point of failure unless it is clustered. DFS Replication synchronizes folder content but does not create a path. Folder Redirection moves user profile folders and does not unify shares behind one path.

q: Two offices have no Azure subscription. Users in both offices edit files in the same shared folder, and either office's file server must be able to serve current files in near real time if the other goes down. What should you configure?
opts: Storage Replica between the two servers' volumes
DFS Namespaces with a folder target on each server and without replication
A scheduled Robocopy /MIR job on a five-minute cycle
DFS Replication between the two servers' shared folders
why: DFS Replication is multi-master and file-level, so changes made in either office flow to the other and both servers can serve current files. Storage Replica is one-way volume replication whose destination volume is not accessible to users until failover. DFS Namespaces alone provides a shared path but leaves the two copies to drift apart. A one-way Robocopy mirror would overwrite or delete changes made on the destination.

q: Four Hyper-V hosts each contain local NVMe and SATA SSDs, and there is no SAN or shared SAS JBOD. You need one pooled storage layer that keeps VMs running if a host fails. What should you deploy?
opts: A Scale-Out File Server role with the default storage configuration
Storage Spaces on a shared SAS JBOD attached to the four hosts
Storage Spaces Direct on a four-node failover cluster
Storage Replica between each pair of hosts
why: Storage Spaces Direct pools the local disks of every cluster node into one software-defined pool and tolerates the loss of a host, which fits hyperconverged hosts with no SAN. Clustered Storage Spaces needs a shared JBOD that these hosts don't have. A Scale-Out File Server is a file-serving role that still needs underlying storage such as Storage Spaces Direct. Storage Replica copies volumes between servers and does not pool local disks.

q: You are asked to enable Data Deduplication on one volume to reclaim space with the lowest risk to performance. Which volume is the best candidate?
opts: A volume that holds live SQL Server data and log files with constant random writes
A volume of already-compressed video archives in which each file is unique
The Windows Server system volume that also hosts the page file
A volume that holds departmental shares and an ISO library with many near-duplicate files
why: Deduplication replaces repeated chunks with references to one stored copy, so it pays off on shares and software libraries full of similar files and is low risk because the data is rarely rewritten. Live database files are heavily and randomly modified, so the overhead outweighs the savings. Already-compressed, unique video offers few duplicate chunks to remove. The system volume is not a supported place to enable it.

q: A branch file server is nearly out of local disk space. Users must still see the full folder structure, including rarely used files, while those files' contents live in Azure. What should you deploy?
opts: The Azure Backup MARS agent protecting the file server's volumes
DFS Replication to a file server virtual machine in Azure
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering disabled, syncing everything to the Azure file share
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled on the server endpoint
why: Cloud tiering keeps the full namespace on the local server but replaces cold files with pointers and streams their content back from Azure on access, which frees local space. Azure File Sync without tiering keeps a full copy of every file locally, so no space is freed. A backup agent protects data for recovery and leaves it all on local disk. DFS Replication to an Azure VM adds a copy but doesn't remove anything from the branch server.

q: While Storage Replica is replicating a volume, users at the destination site cannot access the destination volume.
opts: True
False
why: The destination volume of a Storage Replica partnership is not mounted for normal use while replication is active, and it only becomes available after a failover (a temporary test-failover mount is the exception). This is why Storage Replica suits disaster recovery of a whole volume, while DFS Replication is the choice when users at both ends must work with the files.

q: ReFS can automatically repair a corrupted file only when it can read a good copy from a mirror or parity layout; on a simple, non-resilient space it can detect the corruption but not repair it.
opts: True
False
why: ReFS checksums let it detect corruption on any storage, but repairing it needs a second good copy, which a mirror or parity Storage Spaces layout supplies. On a simple space there is nothing to repair from, so the problem is reported rather than fixed. That is why ReFS is paired with resilient Storage Spaces volumes.

q: Which two statements about Storage Spaces resiliency types are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: A two-way mirror is the most storage-efficient of the resiliency types
A three-way mirror can tolerate two simultaneous drive failures
A simple space survives a drive failure if the pool has a hot spare
Parity suits archive and backup data better than write-heavy transactional workloads
why: A three-way mirror keeps three copies and survives two failures, and parity trades slower random writes for better capacity efficiency, so it fits archives rather than busy databases. A two-way mirror uses half the raw capacity, which is less efficient than parity. A simple space has no redundancy, so a hot spare cannot restore data lost with the failed drive.

q: Which two statements about DFS Namespaces are true? (Choose two.)
opts: A domain-based namespace stores its configuration in AD DS and can use multiple namespace servers
A standalone namespace stores its configuration in AD DS so that clients can find it
Folder targets in a namespace need to be members of a DFS Replication group
A standalone namespace can be made highly available by hosting it on a failover cluster
why: A domain-based namespace keeps its configuration in AD DS and can span several namespace servers for redundancy, while a standalone namespace lives on one server and gets high availability only by being clustered. A standalone namespace keeps its configuration locally rather than in AD. Namespaces and replication are independent: folder targets do not have to replicate.

q: A three-node Hyper-V cluster has a new shared LUN listed in the cluster's Available Storage. Every node must be able to read and write the LUN at the same time, so any node can run any VM without dismounting the disk first. What should you do?
opts: Create a clustered general use file server role on the disk
Assign the disk to a VM's clustered role as a dedicated disk resource
Add the disk to Cluster Shared Volumes by using Add-ClusterSharedVolume
Configure Storage Replica between the disk and a second volume on each node
why: Converting the disk to a Cluster Shared Volume gives every node simultaneous read and write access through a common namespace, so VMs can move between nodes without a dismount and remount. A dedicated disk resource is owned by one node at a time and has to be handed over on failover. A general use file server role is also owned by one node at a time and serves SMB shares rather than shared VM storage. Storage Replica copies a volume to another volume and gives no shared access.

q: Which three statements about shadow copies of shared folders on a Windows Server file server are true? (Choose three.)
opts: Users can restore earlier versions of a file themselves from the Previous Versions tab
By default, shadow copies are stored on the same volume as the data they protect
Shadow copies are enabled per volume, not per individual shared folder
Shadow copies protect the data if the physical disk holding the volume fails
Each shadow copy stores a full duplicate of the volume's data
why: Shadow copies give users self-service recovery through Previous Versions, they are turned on for a whole volume rather than for one share, and by default they are stored on the same volume as the data. That last point is why they are not a backup: a failed disk takes the shadow copies along with the data. Each shadow copy stores only the blocks that changed since the previous one, not a full duplicate.

q: You are creating a Storage Spaces Direct volume for Hyper-V. It must detect and automatically repair silent bit-rot corruption online, without taking the volume offline. How should you configure it?
opts: Format it with NTFS and rely on its self-healing feature
Format it with ReFS on a volume with simple resiliency
Format it with NTFS and schedule a monthly chkdsk run
Format it with ReFS on a mirror-resilient volume
why: ReFS checksums detect silent corruption, and when the volume is mirrored it can fetch a good copy and repair the damage online.
