ReFS on a simple volume still detects problems but has no second copy to repair from. NTFS self-healing fixes file system metadata inconsistencies and has no checksums for file data, so it does not catch bit rot, and an occasional chkdsk run is a manual check rather than automatic online repair.

q: A SQL Server cluster's data volume must be replicated to a building 2 km away, with no committed transaction lost on failover. Separately, staff in two offices edit documents in one shared folder that must stay roughly in sync. Which pairing fits each need?
opts: DFS Replication for the SQL volume; Storage Replica for the shared folder
Synchronous Storage Replica for both the SQL volume and the shared folder
Asynchronous Storage Replica for the SQL volume; DFS Replication for the shared folder
Synchronous Storage Replica for the SQL volume; DFS Replication for the shared folder
why: Synchronous Storage Replica commits writes at both sites before acknowledging them, so no committed transaction is lost, and a short distance keeps latency low enough. Asynchronous mode leaves a small window of possible data loss. DFS Replication is a file-level, multi-master feature that is unsuited to open database files and offers no block-level consistency. Using Storage Replica for the shared folder would leave the second office unable to open the destination volume.

q: Each user has a personal subfolder under D:\Homes. Management wants every subfolder capped at 5 GB with users blocked from exceeding it, and .mp3 files blocked across all of them, without changing NTFS permissions. Which feature should you use?
opts: DFS Namespaces with access-based enumeration enabled
Data Deduplication with .mp3 files excluded from optimization
File Server Resource Manager, with a hard quota template and a file screen
NTFS disk quotas on the D: volume with a per-user limit
why: FSRM quotas cap a folder (a hard quota blocks writes past the limit, and an auto-apply template covers every subfolder), and file screens block specific file types, all without touching NTFS permissions. NTFS disk quotas are volume-wide, based on file ownership, and cannot block file types. Data Deduplication reclaims duplicate data rather than enforcing limits. Access-based enumeration only hides folders users cannot access.

q: A cluster must provide two kinds of file service: VM files for a Hyper-V cluster stored on SMB shares, and home folders for the finance staff. Which role pairing is correct?
opts: Scale-Out File Server for the VM files; a general use file server for the home folders
A general use file server for the VM files; Scale-Out File Server for the home folders
Scale-Out File Server for both the VM files and the home folders
Storage Spaces Direct for the VM files; Scale-Out File Server for the home folders
why: A Scale-Out File Server is active-active on Cluster Shared Volumes and is designed for application data such as Hyper-V and SQL Server over SMB. It is not intended for user documents or home folders, which belong on a general use file server with the features user data needs. Using it for both ignores that limitation, and the other pairings reverse the roles or confuse a storage feature, Storage Spaces Direct, with a file-serving role.

q: A server connects to one iSCSI target through two network adapters. The MPIO feature is installed, but Disk Management shows the same 500 GB LUN as two separate disks. What should you do?
opts: Initialize and format both disks, then take one of them offline
Enable CHAP authentication on the iSCSI target
In the MPIO control panel, add support for iSCSI devices and restart the server
Combine the two adapters into a NIC team and reconnect with a single path
why: MPIO only claims devices it has been told about, so iSCSI devices must be added in the MPIO control panel (Discover Multi-Paths); after the restart the two paths are presented as one MPIO disk with failover and load balancing. Teaming the adapters is not how storage paths are managed for iSCSI. Formatting both disks risks corrupting data because both are the same LUN. CHAP is authentication and has no effect on path aggregation.

q: Employees need their personal documents synchronized between their laptop and desktop from a central on-premises file share, with selective wipe from a lost device. Their profile folders must not be redirected to the server. What should you deploy?
opts: Folder Redirection with Offline Files for the Documents folder
DFS Replication between the user's two devices
Azure File Sync with a server endpoint on each device
Work Folders, with the sync share hosted on the file server
why: Work Folders syncs a user's own files between their devices and a central share, and supports selective wipe of the synced files from a lost device, without redirecting profile folders. Folder Redirection moves the profile folder to the server, which the requirement forbids. Azure File Sync keeps servers in sync with an Azure file share and uses Windows Server endpoints, not user devices. DFS Replication replicates server folders and is not a per-user device sync.

q: Which two statements about thin provisioning in Storage Spaces are correct? (Choose two.)
opts: Thin provisioning adds new physical disks to the storage pool when its capacity runs low
Fixed provisioning lets the combined disk sizes exceed the pool's physical capacity
When the pool runs out of physical capacity, writes to thin disks fail while Windows still shows free space
A thin virtual disk can be created with a size larger than the pool's free capacity
why: Thin disks consume pool capacity only as data is written, so their combined size can exceed the pool, but that makes real pool capacity something to monitor: when it is exhausted, writes fail while the volumes still report free space. Thin provisioning never adds disks by itself, and over-allocation is the thin behavior, since a fixed disk reserves its full size when it is created.

q: Hybrid users synced from AD DS to Microsoft Entra ID need read and write access to an Azure file share, and only the Sales group may change files in the Sales folder. What is the correct permission model?
opts: Assign only Windows ACLs, because share-level permissions are never needed once an identity source is enabled
Distribute the storage account key to the users and restrict folders with a shared access signature
Assign the Owner role on the storage account to the group
Assign a Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor role to the users' group at share level and set Windows ACLs on the Sales folder
why: Identity-based access needs a share-level permission through Azure RBAC and then directory and file permissions through Windows ACLs for granularity. The storage account key bypasses identity entirely, ACLs alone are not enough without a share-level permission (or default permission), and Owner grants control-plane control of the account rather than file access.

q: Which two statements about identity-based authentication for Azure Files over SMB are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Computer accounts, which have no Microsoft Entra identity, can reach a share through a default share-level permission
AD DS and Microsoft Entra Domain Services can both be enabled on the same storage account at once
Share-level permissions are enforced through Windows ACLs on each folder
Only one identity source can be used per storage account, and it applies to all its file shares
why: A storage account uses a single identity source for all its shares, and the default share-level permission is how identities that do not exist in Entra ID, such as computer accounts, get access. Two sources cannot be active together, and Windows ACLs enforce directory and file permissions, while share-level permissions come from Azure RBAC or the default permission.

q: In the Storage Sync Service, a registered server shows the state Appears Offline. Which is a documented cause?
opts: Cloud tiering has recalled too many files to the server
The server's agent version has been promoted to the latest release
The Storage Sync Monitor process is not running, or the server cannot reach the Azure File Sync service
The Azure file share has exceeded its quota
why: The registered server health reflects whether the monitor process runs and the server can reach the service; otherwise it appears offline. Tiering and recall activity, share quota, and a newer agent would show up as errors or version warnings rather than an offline server.

q: A team migrates a DFS Replication group to Azure File Sync while both run on the same server for a time. Which precaution is required?
opts: Stop DFS Namespaces, because they cannot be used with Azure File Sync
Create server endpoints on the DFS-R read-only replicated folders to protect the data
Enable cloud tiering on every volume first so that DFS-R sees less data
Disable cloud tiering on volumes that hold DFS-R replicated folders, and overlap only one server endpoint with a DFS-R location
why: While both replicate, cloud tiering must be off on volumes with DFS-R folders, only a single server endpoint should overlap a DFS-R location, and server endpoints should not be created on read-only DFS-R folders. DFS Namespaces work fully with Azure File Sync and can continue to provide the namespace.

q: Field staff on the Internet must open files on a Windows Server 2025 file server without a VPN. The firewall team asks which inbound rule to create. What should they allow, and what must they not expose?
opts: Allow TCP 443 and TCP 5985 inbound for QUIC and WinRM
Allow UDP 500 and UDP 4500 for IPsec NAT traversal
Allow TCP 445 inbound because SMB over QUIC still uses the legacy port
Allow UDP 443 inbound for SMB over QUIC, and do not allow TCP 445 inbound
why: SMB over QUIC wraps SMB in a TLS 1.3 tunnel on UDP port 443, so only that port is allowed inbound, and TCP 445 must stay closed to the Internet. Port 445 is the legacy transport, TCP 443 is not what QUIC uses, and 500/4500 belong to IPsec VPNs. It also needs a server certificate and a Windows 11 client.

q: SMB over QUIC is enabled by default on Windows Server 2025, and clients attempt it before TCP.
opts: True
False
why: An administrator must opt in on the file server, and a client cannot force a server to enable it. Windows SMB clients still try TCP first and use QUIC only if TCP fails or the user requires it, for example with net use /transport:quic.

q: Windows Server 2025 requires both inbound and outbound SMB signing by default.
opts: True
False
why: Windows Server 2025 requires outbound SMB signing only by default. Windows 11 version 24H2 Pro, Enterprise, and Education require both inbound and outbound signing, and Home edition requires neither.

q: Under Storage QoS, a virtual machine issues a single 256 KB read. How many normalized IOPS does that request count as?
why: Storage QoS normalizes IO to 8 KB: any IO of 8 KB or smaller counts as one, and larger IOs count as multiple, so 256 KB is 32 normalized IOs. Counting it as one ignores the size, and 8 and 256 do not correspond to dividing by 8 KB.

q: You must allow only approved executables to run on a fleet of Windows Server 2022 file servers. The control must keep blocking unapproved code even if an attacker gains local administrator rights and tries to turn it off. Which technology should you deploy?
opts: Windows Defender Application Control with an enforced code integrity policy
Just Enough Administration endpoints for the file server administrators
Software Restriction Policies with a default disallowed rule
AppLocker with enforced executable rules
why: WDAC enforces a code integrity policy in the kernel for the whole system, so a local administrator cannot simply switch it off. AppLocker and Software Restriction Policies are user-mode rule engines that a privileged attacker can work around or disable far more easily. JEA limits what an administrator can do in a PowerShell session but does not stop arbitrary executables from running.

q: An attacker with local administrator rights on a domain-joined server uses Mimikatz to dump NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets from LSASS memory. You need a control that still protects those secrets even if the attacker loads a kernel-mode driver. Which feature should you enable?
opts: Protected Users group membership for the administrators
Remote Credential Guard
Credential Guard
BitLocker with a TPM protector
why: Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to keep LSASS secrets in a hypervisor-isolated container that even kernel-level code in the normal OS cannot read. Remote Credential Guard protects credentials during Remote Desktop sessions by redirecting Kerberos requests to the client and does not isolate LSASS on the server. Protected Users restricts how accounts authenticate but does not shield memory. BitLocker protects data at rest and has no effect on secrets in memory.

q: You will use Windows LAPS to store local administrator passwords for Windows Server 2025 member servers in Active Directory, retrievable by the help desk. Before configuring the policy, what must you do in the domain?
opts: Enable the AD Recycle Bin in the forest
Install the legacy LAPS MSI package on the member servers
Create a group managed service account for the help desk
Extend the AD schema by running Update-LapsADSchema
why: Windows LAPS stores passwords in new AD attributes, so the schema must be extended with Update-LapsADSchema; you then grant computers permission to update their own password and delegate who can read it. Windows LAPS is built into current Windows Server, so the legacy LAPS MSI is not needed and uses different attributes. A gMSA is for service accounts, and the Recycle Bin is unrelated to password storage.

q: A regulated company wants Windows Server security events and Microsoft Defender for Identity alerts correlated with its cloud workload alerts in one security operations view, using custom analytics rules and automated response playbooks. Which service should ingest the data?
opts: A Windows Event Forwarding collector server
Microsoft Sentinel
Microsoft Defender for Cloud, using its secure score and recommendations
A Log Analytics workspace with log alert rules alone
why: Microsoft Sentinel is the cloud-native SIEM and SOAR that ingests many sources, correlates them with analytics rules into incidents, and runs playbooks for response. Defender for Cloud focuses on posture and workload protection for resources rather than being a general SIEM. A Windows Event Forwarding collector only centralizes Windows events. A Log Analytics workspace with log alerts stores and queries data but lacks Sentinel's incident correlation and playbook orchestration.

q: A device can back up its Windows LAPS password to both Active Directory and Microsoft Entra ID at the same time.
opts: True
False
why: Windows LAPS policy selects a single backup directory for a device: disabled, Microsoft Entra ID, or Active Directory. A hybrid-joined device must therefore be configured for one of them. The choice depends on how the device is joined and where the help desk will retrieve the password.

q: A member of the Protected Users group cannot sign in to a domain-joined laptop while it is offline, because that account's credentials are not cached on the device.
opts: True
False
why: Protected Users blocks credential caching, so a laptop has no cached sign-in verifier for the account and the user must reach a domain controller to authenticate. The group also forces Kerberos, blocks NTLM, and disables delegation. That offline side effect is one reason it is reserved for high-privilege accounts rather than every user.

q: Which two statements about Microsoft Defender for Identity are true? (Choose two.)
opts: It can alert on on-premises attack techniques such as pass-the-hash and DCSync
Its sensors are installed on domain controllers to observe on-premises AD DS traffic
It detects risky sign-ins for cloud-only users who have no on-premises account
It requires a sensor on the member servers to detect lateral movement
why: Defender for Identity runs sensors on domain controllers and is built to detect on-premises identity attacks such as reconnaissance, pass-the-hash, and DCSync. Risky sign-ins for cloud-only users are the job of Microsoft Entra ID Protection. Sensors go on domain controllers (and certain identity servers), not on every member server.

q: In a JEA session, commands run under a temporary virtual account, but the session logs still record the identity of the user who connected.
opts: True
False
why: JEA runs the permitted cmdlets as a virtual account (or a gMSA) so the connecting user needs no administrator rights, yet transcripts and event logs capture who connected and what they ran, which preserves accountability. The user never receives general administrative access.

q: A hardened server has both Windows LAPS and Credential Guard deployed. An attacker who gains local administrator rights on that server tries to (1) look up the local administrator's own password, and (2) extract other users' cached credentials from LSASS memory using a tool like Mimikatz. Which of these two actions does Credential Guard block?
opts: Only the LSASS credential-extraction attempt (2); Credential Guard has no bearing on LAPS-managed password storage or retrieval
Both actions (1) and (2), since Credential Guard supersedes LAPS entirely
Only the LAPS password lookup (1); Credential Guard has no effect on LSASS credential extraction
Neither action, since Credential Guard only protects Kerberos tickets, not NTLM or other LSASS secrets
why: Credential Guard isolates LSASS secrets, including cached NTLM and Kerberos credentials, inside a virtualization-based security container, blocking Mimikatz-style extraction — but it has nothing to do with where or how LAPS stores or exposes the local administrator password, which is retrieved through Entra ID or AD DS delegation instead. Credential Guard also protects more than just Kerberos tickets; it covers NTLM secrets held in LSASS too.

q: A security team wants a help-desk technician to be able to restart a specific set of services and clear specific event logs on a file server, under an elevated identity, but must not grant that technician's own account general local administrator rights on the box. Which feature should be configured?
opts: Just Enough Administration (JEA), with a role capability file scoped to those cmdlets
The Protected Users security group, applied to the technician's own account
Windows LAPS, so the technician can retrieve the local administrator password on demand
Add the technician to the local Administrators group and restrict tools with AppLocker rules
why: JEA constrains a PowerShell session to a defined set of cmdlets and parameters through a role capability file and runs them under a virtual account, so the technician can do exactly those tasks without administrator rights. Local Administrators membership grants broad access that AppLocker rules only partly restrict. Windows LAPS hands the technician the administrator password, which is full administrative access. Protected Users restricts how an account authenticates and not what it is allowed to do.

q: Domain administrator accounts must be allowed to sign in only from privileged access workstations and domain controllers, and their Kerberos ticket-granting ticket lifetime must be shortened. Which feature should you configure?
opts: The Protected Users security group for those accounts
An authentication policy with an authentication policy silo
A fine-grained password policy applied to those accounts
Credential Guard enabled on the workstations
why: Authentication policies restrict where an account may authenticate from, can set a custom Kerberos TGT lifetime, and silos group the accounts with the devices they may use. Protected Users forces stronger Kerberos and a fixed short ticket lifetime but does not limit which machines an account can sign in from. A fine-grained password policy changes password and lockout rules only. Credential Guard protects secrets in memory and does not restrict sign-in locations.

q: You are designing a two-tier PKI. The root CA must stay powered off except when it signs or revokes a subordinate CA certificate. The issuing CA must support autoenrollment of computer certificates through certificate templates and Group Policy. Which CA types should you deploy?
opts: A standalone root CA for the root; a standalone subordinate CA for issuing
An enterprise root CA for the root; an enterprise subordinate CA for issuing
An enterprise root CA for the root; a standalone subordinate CA for issuing
A standalone root CA for the root; an enterprise subordinate CA for issuing
why: An enterprise CA depends on AD DS and must stay online and domain-joined to read templates, so the offline root is a standalone CA, while the issuing CA must be an enterprise CA because autoenrollment through templates and Group Policy is an enterprise feature. An enterprise root cannot realistically sit powered off. A standalone issuing CA has no template or autoenrollment support and needs manual approval of each request.

q: When the root CA is kept offline, its certificate revocation list must be published manually to a location that clients can reach, because the root CA itself is not available to serve it.
opts: True
False
why: An offline root CA cannot answer CRL requests, so its CRL, usually issued with a long validity period, is exported and published to an accessible distribution point. If clients cannot retrieve a valid CRL, chain validation can fail. This operational detail is the price of keeping the root CA's key protected.

q: A server that is not joined to a domain must be hardened with Microsoft's published security baseline settings for its Windows Server version. Which tool from the Security Compliance Toolkit applies those settings to the local server?
opts: LGPO.exe
Policy Analyzer
The Security Configuration Wizard
The Import Settings feature in the Group Policy Management Console
why: LGPO.exe, the Local Group Policy Object utility in the toolkit, imports baseline settings into a server's local policy, so it works without a domain. Policy Analyzer only compares baselines and GPOs against each other and applies nothing. The GPMC import feature loads a baseline into a domain GPO, which requires a domain. The Security Configuration Wizard builds role-based security policy and is not part of the toolkit's baselines.

q: A security team wants to enable exploit protection mitigations on a fleet of servers without breaking applications. Which sequence is recommended?
opts: Import an EMET profile, because EMET is the supported tool on current Windows Server
Enable only SmartScreen, which includes all exploit mitigations
Enable every mitigation system-wide in enforce mode and fix breakage as tickets arrive
Test in audit mode, export the configuration as XML, and deploy it with Group Policy
why: Audit mode logs what would be blocked so you can add app-specific exceptions before enforcement, and the exported XML can be distributed by Group Policy. Enforcing everything at once risks outages, SmartScreen is reputation protection rather than exploit mitigation, and EMET reached end of support in 2018 and is replaced by exploit protection.

q: A Windows Server 2025 fleet must keep a role-aware security baseline, Defender Antivirus settings, and LAPS configuration, with unauthorized local changes corrected automatically. Azure Policy should take precedence over local tools. Which feature fits?
opts: OSConfig with drift control turned on
A scheduled task that exports local policy to a file share
Microsoft Defender SmartScreen
Group Policy preferences with item-level targeting
why: OSConfig applies scenarios such as the security baseline, Defender Antivirus, and LAPS, detects and corrects drift, and orders authorities with Azure Policy first. Group Policy preferences apply settings but do not continuously correct drift in this way, SmartScreen is reputation filtering, and exporting policy to a file share only records state.

q: OSConfig security configuration is available on Windows Server 2022 as well as Windows Server 2025.
opts: True
False
why: The OSConfig documentation applies to Windows Server 2025. On earlier versions, baselines are applied with other tools such as Group Policy and the Security Compliance Toolkit, without OSConfig's drift control.

q: Which two statements about on-premises Microsoft Entra Password Protection are true? (Choose two.)
opts: The proxy service must be installed on each domain controller
Users' clear-text passwords are sent to Microsoft Entra ID for checking
Domain controllers never need to communicate directly with the internet
The policy is enforced only by domain controllers that run the DC agent
why: A proxy service on a domain-joined member server fetches policy for the DCs, so DCs stay off the internet, and only DCs with the agent validate password changes. The proxy is not installed on DCs, and clear-text passwords never leave the DC because validation uses the locally cached policy.

q: File servers must accept SMB connections only from domain computers that have authenticated to them with IPsec. What should the administrator configure?
opts: A DHCP reservation for each authorized client
A connection security rule requiring authentication, with a firewall rule that allows SMB only if the connection is secure
A firewall rule that blocks all inbound traffic, with no other rules
An exploit protection setting for the Server service
why: Connection security rules require IPsec authentication between computers, and a firewall rule set to allow only secure connections enforces it. Blocking everything breaks the service, exploit protection hardens processes rather than authenticating peers, and reservations only fix addresses.

q: The help desk must reset passwords only for users in the Marketing OU and must not hold membership in Account Operators or Domain Admins. What should the administrator do?
opts: Run the Delegation of Control Wizard on the Marketing OU for the help desk group, granting Reset user passwords
Add the help desk group to Domain Admins temporarily
Give the help desk group the Replicating Directory Changes permission
Grant the help desk group Full Control on the domain root
why: Delegating a specific task on one OU applies least privilege. Domain Admins and Full Control on the domain root grant far more than needed, and Replicating Directory Changes allows reading directory data for replication, not resetting passwords.

q: The AdminSDHolder process re-applies a protected security descriptor to privileged accounts and groups about every 60 minutes, so a manual permission change on a Domain Admins member is overwritten.
opts: True
False
why: AdminSDHolder and SDProp periodically reset the ACL on protected accounts and groups, which is why delegated permissions set on such objects disappear and why privileged accounts should not be used for ordinary delegated administration.

q: A server has intermittent CPU spikes. Using only built-in local tools and no Azure services, you want detailed counters and a trace captured only while CPU stays above 90 percent. What should you configure?
opts: A Data Collector Set whose counter alert starts a second Data Collector Set
A metric alert rule with an action group in Azure Monitor
A scheduled Data Collector Set that records continuously, reviewed weekly
Reliability Monitor with a stability index threshold alert
why: A performance counter alert inside a Data Collector Set can run a task, including starting another Data Collector Set, when a counter crosses a threshold, which captures detail only during the spike with no cloud dependency. A metric alert with an action group needs Azure Monitor. A continuously recording set captures everything rather than just the spike. Reliability Monitor tracks a stability index, not performance counters, and cannot trigger collection.

q: You want to collect Windows security events from 30 on-premises servers into a Log Analytics workspace by using Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule. The servers are not currently connected to Azure. What must be true before you can associate the rule with them?
opts: Each server must be Azure Arc-enabled so that it exists as an Azure resource
Each server must run the legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent first
Each server must be reachable from Azure over a site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute
Each server must be hybrid joined to Microsoft Entra ID
why: A data collection rule is associated with Azure resources, and Azure Arc is what turns an on-premises server into one and delivers Azure Monitor Agent to it as an extension. Hybrid join concerns identity and does not create an Azure resource. Arc agents connect outbound, so no VPN or ExpressRoute is required. The legacy MMA agent is what Azure Monitor Agent replaces and is not a prerequisite.

q: A Log Analytics workspace holds Windows event data. What does this KQL query return? Event | where EventLog == "System" and EventLevelName == "Error" | summarize Count = count() by Computer | order by Count desc
opts: Each System error event, grouped by computer and sorted by time
The most recent System error event from each computer
One row per computer with its number of System error events, highest first
A single row with the total number of System errors across the computers
why: where filters to System-log errors, summarize count() by Computer collapses the rows to one per computer holding its error count, and order by Count desc ranks them. Returning the latest event per computer would need a different aggregation such as arg_max. Without by Computer, summarize would produce one total row. Because summarize aggregates, the individual events are not returned, so listing every event sorted by time is not what this query does.

q: You manage 300 Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. They must be patched in a Saturday window, and machines tagged Env=Prod must be included automatically as they are added, without editing a server list. What should you use?
opts: WSUS with computer groups and an automatic approval rule for each group
Azure Update Manager maintenance configuration with a tag-based dynamic scope
Cluster-Aware Updating with a self-updating schedule on each server
An Azure Automation runbook that patches a static list of server names
why: Update Manager maintenance configurations schedule patching across Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers, and a dynamic scope selects machines by criteria such as tags when the run starts, so new Env=Prod machines are picked up automatically. WSUS groups are not driven by Azure tags. A runbook with a static list needs editing for every new server. Cluster-Aware Updating orchestrates patching of failover cluster nodes only.

q: A server crashes intermittently. Before reading detailed logs, you want a quick timeline that shows a stability index and lines up each crash with recent software installs and updates. Which tool should you open first?
opts: Resource Monitor
Reliability Monitor
The Event Viewer System log
The Performance Monitor System Diagnostics report
why: Reliability Monitor plots a stability index over time and annotates it with installs, updates, and failures, which shows when the problem began. Event Viewer holds the detailed events that confirm the cause afterward but offers no correlated timeline. Resource Monitor shows live resource use, and the System Diagnostics report is a point-in-time snapshot of configuration and counters.

q: Azure Update Manager can assess and patch an on-premises Windows Server over an Azure VPN connection, without the server being Azure Arc-enabled.
opts: True
False
why: Network connectivity to Azure does not make a server visible to Update Manager. The server must be an Azure VM or an Azure Arc-enabled server so that it exists as an Azure resource. A plain on-premises server with only a VPN link to Azure still needs the Arc agent, or a separate tool such as WSUS.

q: A single machine can be associated with several data collection rules at the same time, for example one that collects performance counters and another that collects security events.
opts: True
False
why: Associations are many-to-many: one rule can apply to many machines, and one machine can have several rules, each defining its own data sources and destinations. That lets teams author small, purpose-specific rules and combine them per server role instead of maintaining one oversized rule.

q: Which two statements about Azure Monitor alert rules and action groups are true? (Choose two.)
opts: Each alert rule embeds its own notification settings instead of using shared action groups
One action group can be referenced by many different alert rules
A log alert rule runs a KQL query on a schedule and fires based on the query results
A metric alert rule is defined by a KQL query over a Log Analytics workspace
why: Log alerts evaluate a scheduled KQL query, and action groups exist so one response, such as paging on-call, can be reused by many alert rules. A metric alert evaluates a numeric signal against a threshold and is not defined by a KQL query. Notification settings are kept in action groups precisely so they do not have to be embedded in every rule.

q: A server restarted unexpectedly three times last week. Which two actions help you determine when the restarts began and why they happened? (Choose two.)
opts: Review Reliability Monitor for the stability index drop and nearby installs
Create a Data Collector Set with memory counters and review last week's history
Run Best Practices Analyzer against the file server role to check its settings
Filter the System log in Event Viewer for Event ID 41 (Kernel-Power)
why: Reliability Monitor gives the timeline and correlates it with installs and updates, and the System log records the unexpected-shutdown events that confirm each restart. Best Practices Analyzer checks a role's configuration rules and says nothing about past restarts. A Data Collector Set only records from the moment it starts, so it cannot reconstruct last week.

q: A team wants Security and Application event log entries from 50 servers centralized onto a single collector server for review, without deploying Azure Monitor Agent or a Log Analytics workspace, using only built-in Windows Server functionality. Which feature should be configured?
opts: Data Collector Sets, configured on the collector server and pointed at each of the 50 servers over WMI
Reliability Monitor, configured on the collector server to poll each of the 50 servers' stability index remotely
Windows Event Forwarding (WEF), using a subscription on the collector server and WinRM on each source server
Azure Update Manager, using its centralized reporting dashboard to pull patch and event data from each server
why: Windows Event Forwarding uses WinRM-based subscriptions so a collector server can gather selected event log entries from many source servers into its own forwarded-events log, entirely with built-in Windows Server functionality and no Azure agent required. Data Collector Sets on the collector alone wouldn't gather anything from the other 50 servers, since they capture local performance and trace data. Reliability Monitor only tracks a single server's own stability index locally. Update Manager is a patch-compliance service, unrelated to centralizing event logs.

q: An operations team manages a hybrid fleet of Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers and wants a single view showing each server's running processes, discovered application dependencies, and connections to other servers, to help plan a migration and troubleshoot cross-server issues. Which Azure Monitor capability provides this?
opts: VM insights, using the dependency map feature
Reliability Monitor on each server
Azure Update Manager compliance reports
Change Tracking and Inventory reports
why: The VM insights dependency map, which relies on the Dependency Agent alongside Azure Monitor Agent, visualizes running processes and the connections between servers across Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers. Change Tracking and Inventory records software, file, and registry changes and an inventory, but does not map connections between machines. Update Manager reports patch compliance, and Reliability Monitor is a single-server stability timeline.

q: A team wants to be paged within a minute if a server's disk queue length spikes, and separately wants a weekly report correlating that same spike with any application deployments that happened around the same time. Which combination of Azure Monitor capabilities fits each need respectively?
opts: An activity log alert for the page; a data collection rule for the weekly correlation report
A metric alert on disk queue length for the page; a scheduled KQL query joining performance and deployment data for the report
A log alert running a KQL query once a minute for the page; a Data Collector Set for the weekly correlation report
A metric alert for both needs, since a metric alert can also join deployment records from other tables
why: Metric alerts evaluate lightweight numeric thresholds quickly enough for near-real-time paging, while a scheduled KQL query that joins performance and deployment data in Log Analytics suits a periodic, multi-source correlation report. A log alert every minute depends on ingestion latency and a heavier query, and a Data Collector Set only captures local counters and cannot produce a correlation report. A metric alert evaluates one numeric signal and cannot join tables. The activity log records Azure control-plane operations, not disk counters, and a data collection rule only defines what is collected and where it goes.

q: You configure Windows Event Forwarding so a collector receives Security events from 200 source servers by using a source-initiated subscription. Which two actions are required for the sources to forward the Security log? (Choose two.)
opts: Run wecutil qc on each source server to enable the forwarding service
Add NETWORK SERVICE to the Event Log Readers group on each source
Allow inbound TCP 5985 through the firewall of each source server
Apply a GPO setting that points the sources to the collector
why: In a source-initiated subscription a GPO tells every source where its subscription manager is, so the 200 servers need no individual setup, and the forwarding service account (NETWORK SERVICE) needs rights to read the Security log through Event Log Readers membership. wecutil qc prepares the collector, not the sources. In a source-initiated design the sources connect outbound to the collector, so the inbound WinRM port matters on the collector rather than on every source.

q: Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule alone is enough to populate the VM insights dependency map.
opts: True
False
why: Azure Monitor Agent collects logs and performance counters, which gives VM insights its performance views, but the dependency map needs the separate Dependency Agent to discover process-level connections between servers. Without it you still get performance data but not the map.

q: After promoting a new domain controller, you want to run a Best Practices Analyzer scan of its AD DS role from PowerShell. Which cmdlet starts the scan?
opts: Test-ADDSDomainControllerInstallation for the new server
Invoke-BpaModel with the DirectoryServices model ID
Get-ADDomainController -Discover to locate the server
Get-BpaResult for the DirectoryServices model
why: Invoke-BpaModel runs a Best Practices Analyzer scan for a given model, here the Directory Services model. Get-BpaResult only reads the results of a scan that has already been run. Test-ADDSDomainControllerInstallation checks prerequisites before a promotion and not the role's configuration afterward, and Get-ADDomainController -Discover locates a domain controller and runs no analysis.

q: Change Tracking and Inventory for an on-premises server requires the legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent.
opts: True
False
why: Change Tracking and Inventory is delivered through Azure Monitor Agent and a data collection rule, and works for Azure VMs and Arc-enabled on-premises servers alike. The legacy Log Analytics (MMA) agent is what Azure Monitor Agent replaced, so it is not required.

q: An administrator wants local, machine-learning-based warnings that a data volume will fill in a few weeks, without sending data to the cloud. Which feature provides it?
opts: Reliability Monitor
System Insights volume consumption forecasting
Performance Monitor with a data collector set
Azure Monitor VM insights
why: System Insights forecasts volume, total storage, CPU, and network usage locally and writes predictions to the event log. A data collector set records current counters but does not predict, VM insights sends data to Azure Monitor, and Reliability Monitor reports stability events.

q: Windows Update on a server fails, and the admin needs a readable log. Which statement is correct?
opts: Run Get-WindowsUpdateLog, which merges the .etl trace files into a static WindowsUpdate.log
Query the Security event log for update errors
Run repadmin /showrepl on the server
Open WindowsUpdate.log, which is continuously updated in plain text
why: Modern Windows writes Windows Update traces to .etl files, and Get-WindowsUpdateLog converts them to a WindowsUpdate.log that is a snapshot and must be regenerated to reflect new activity. The plain-text live log is the old behavior, and the Security log and repadmin do not report update agent errors.

q: Encrypting an Azure VM with Azure Disk Encryption fails with 'Failed to send DiskEncryptionData'. Which is a documented cause to check first?
opts: The VM's SMB signing setting is not required, so the encryption extension refuses to send keys
The domain functional level is below Windows Server 2016, so BitLocker cannot escrow the key
The Key Vault is in a different region or subscription than the VM, or its access policies do not allow Azure Disk Encryption
The VM sits in an availability set with more than five update domains configured
why: ADE requires the Key Vault to be in the same region and subscription as the VM and to have access policies enabling disk encryption, and a disabled or missing key encryption key or a typo in identifiers also cause this error. SMB signing, functional levels, and update domains are unrelated.

q: A team is planning new Azure VMs and wants all temporary disks and disk caches encrypted at rest, with a path that avoids the retiring in-guest encryption feature. What should they choose?
opts: SMB encryption on the VM's file shares
Encryption at host
Azure Disk Encryption, because it will be supported indefinitely
Storage Spaces mirroring
why: Encryption at host encrypts temp disks and caches and is the recommended option for new VMs, while Azure Disk Encryption is scheduled for retirement on September 15, 2028, after which encrypted disks fail to unlock after reboots. Storage Spaces mirroring is resiliency, and SMB encryption protects traffic in transit.

q: Users cannot open a file share on FS01 from a branch client. The client's ping to FS01 succeeds. Which command best tests whether the SMB port is reachable?
opts: Test-NetConnection -ComputerName FS01 -Port 445
w32tm /resync
ipconfig /renew
ping FS01 -t
why: Test-NetConnection with -Port tests a specific TCP port, which separates a firewall or service problem from a name or address problem. Ping tests only ICMP, which already works, and renewing the lease or resyncing time does not test the SMB port.

q: After an administrator changes a server's DNS record, one client keeps connecting to the old address. Other clients are fine. Which action on the affected client is the best first step?
opts: Reinstall the DHCP role on the client
Run dcdiag on the client
Reset the client's computer account password
Run ipconfig /flushdns and test with Resolve-DnsName against the intended DNS server
why: A stale entry in the client's DNS cache explains a single client resolving to the old address, and querying the intended server with Resolve-DnsName confirms what the server returns. dcdiag tests domain controllers, a computer account reset addresses trust failures, and the client has no DHCP server role to reinstall.
